title: Design a Meal Delivery Service
brief: Customers find restaurants near them, order food, pay, and watch a courier approach on a map. Couriers report their position constantly, and each restaurant gets the order on a tablet. Dinner time is several times busier than the afternoon, and a dish that is nearly sold out must not be sold to two people.
constraints: Finding restaurants and placing an order must each respond within 400 ms; the payment processor alone takes about a quarter of a second
About 6,000 requests per second at peak, and three times that at dinner
Placing an order twice by accident (a double tap) creates one order
A dish with one portion left is sold to one person
Customers are charged through an external payment processor, and restaurants are told through an external messaging provider
Live courier tracking is nice to have, but ordering must work without it
About 3 million dishes from 100,000 restaurants, and 150 million orders from 20 million customers

capabilities.label: Find restaurants nearby
capabilities.hint: List open restaurants close to the customer, with their menus

capabilities.label: Place an order
capabilities.hint: Create the order and take the dishes out of stock. A double tap must make one order, and the last portion must go to one person.

capabilities.label: Charge the customer
capabilities.hint: Take payment through the processor when an order is placed

capabilities.label: Record courier positions
capabilities.hint: Keep the courier's position current so the customer can watch the map

capabilities.label: Send the order to the restaurant
capabilities.hint: Tell the restaurant's tablet about the new order

queries.label: Check how many portions of the dish are left
Look for the customer's open order, in case of a double tap

scenarios.title: Typical peak
scenarios.description: Steady browsing with the usual rate of orders.
scenarios.interviewQuestion: Browsing near me, ordering, and courier tracking behave very differently. Which of them share a service and which should not?
scenarios.debrief: Browsing is cache and index reads; ordering is a small, locked, idempotent write path.

scenarios.title: Dinner rush (3x)
scenarios.interviewQuestion: Which part feels the dinner rush first, and which parts can wait a few seconds?
scenarios.debrief: Autoscaling widens the busy services, and the queue keeps restaurant notification from blocking orders.

scenarios.title: Courier tracking hangs
scenarios.description: Whatever runs courier tracking becomes 15x slower.
scenarios.interviewQuestion: Tracking hangs. Should an order wait for it, and what happens to the map the customer sees?
scenarios.debrief: Courier tracking is its own service, so its slowdown never touches browsing or ordering.

scenarios.title: Restaurant messaging outage
scenarios.description: The external messaging provider stops answering.
scenarios.interviewQuestion: Restaurants cannot be told about orders. Do you still accept orders, and how do restaurants find out?
scenarios.debrief: Orders succeed regardless, because notification is asynchronous and optional.

requirements.text: Browsing and ordering meet the latency target at peak
Restaurants and couriers are in a geographic index
Something places orders, once, and never oversells a dish
A hung courier tracker does not slow ordering
Ordering keeps working when restaurant messaging is down
The design explains how the last portion of a dish is protected
Every query is answered through a key or an index, never by reading a whole table

rubric: Restaurants and courier positions are in a geographic index; browsing reads it through a cache.
Placing an order is idempotent (an order key) and decrements stock with a lock or conditional write.
Payment and restaurant notification are separate steps; the payment is essential and idempotent, while restaurant notification is optional and isolated so its outage does not stop orders.
Courier tracking is high volume and optional, isolated so it cannot slow ordering.
Dinner-time scaling uses autoscaling on the busy parts rather than permanent capacity everywhere.

reference.summary: Separate browsing, ordering and tracking, protect orders with idempotency and stock locks, and keep restaurant messaging optional.
design: User, then a Load Balancer that routes by request class: a Browse Server (7 replicas, autoscale) reading a Cache in front of a Geo Index (quadtree, 3 areas); an Order Service (idempotency keys, Row locks) writing the Database; a Tracking Service updating the Geo Index.
The Order Service calls a Payment Service (idempotency keys) that charges through a Third-party API set to Payment processor.
It also sends the order to a Queue asynchronously; a Worker tells the restaurant through a Third-party API set to Email / SMS.
tradeoffs: Tracking in its own service costs a little and keeps a hung tracker from slowing orders.
Payment is essential and has no fallback; restaurant notification is optional and can fail without losing orders.
